judgments.yea_description: Voted yes to accept the Senate's version of LD 1126, a gun serial-number bill. The Maine House agreed 73-67, then enacted the bill the same day. It became law without the governor's signature in January 2026, as Public Law Chapter 537. The law bars knowingly having, bringing into Maine, or transferring a gun, frame, or receiver with no serial number. Buying a serial-numbered frame or receiver requires a background check. Antique guns, collector items, permanently disabled guns, and guns made before 1968 are exempt. Making, selling, or knowingly having a gun that security screening cannot detect is also a crime. Penalties start January 1, 2027.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1126, a gun bill. A serial number is the maker's ID number that lets police trace a gun. Starting January 1, 2027, having a gun with no serial number is a civil violation with a fine of up to $50 the first time, and a crime for repeat offenses. Bringing one into Maine, selling it, or handing it over is a crime from the first offense. The rules also cover the frame, the core part a gun is built on. Buying one that already has a number requires a background check. Guns made before 1968, antiques, collector pieces, and guns that can no longer fire are left out. The bill also bans guns built to slip past metal detectors. This was the final passage vote. The Maine Senate passed it 17-16 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1971, a bill about local police and federal immigration agents. Maine police, sheriffs, and jails may no longer spend their money or their officers' time helping enforce federal civil immigration law. They may not hold someone in jail past their release time just because federal agents ask. They may not tell those agents a person's release date or home address unless that information is already public. They may still share someone's immigration status when federal law calls for it, and they may still run normal criminal investigations. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 75-73 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 538, a bill about what goes on a prescription label. A pharmacy may now print the name of the health care facility on the label instead of the name of the prescriber, meaning the doctor, nurse practitioner, or other provider who wrote the prescription. This applies to mifepristone and misoprostol, the drugs used for medication abortion, and to their generic versions. It happens only if the prescriber asks for it. Normally Maine law requires the prescriber's own name on every drug label. The Maine House passed it 75-71 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 556, a bill about who decides what heats your home. A Maine town or city may no longer pass a rule that stops a person or business from picking any safe heating or energy system sold on the market. Towns also may not block someone from hiring a fuel or energy company to install, service, or refill that system. Towns may still encourage one kind of system and spend money to promote it. In practice this stops a town from banning natural gas or oil heat in new buildings. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 78-67 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1868, a clean electricity bill. Companies that sell electricity in Maine must start buying power the state counts as clean. The share starts at 1 percent of what they sell in 2031 and climbs to 10 percent by 2040. Nuclear plants count. So do hydroelectric dams that meet the state's rules for letting fish swim past. So does any power the state certifies as giving off almost no greenhouse gas. The law also raises the separate renewable power requirement from 40 percent in 2030 to 50 percent by 2040. It moves the state's goal from 100 percent renewable electricity by 2050 to 90 percent renewable plus 10 percent clean by 2040. If enough clean power is not built, the Public Utilities Commission may pause the scheduled increases. This was the final passage vote. The Maine House passed it 77-68 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 61, a bill about bosses watching workers. A boss must tell workers before starting to watch them with computers, phones, or other electronic monitoring systems. Security or safety cameras, and GPS tracking on company-owned vehicles, do not count as surveillance under this law. The boss must tell job applicants at the interview and give current workers written notice once a year. Watching or recording a worker inside their home, their own car, or on their own property is banned unless the job truly requires it. Workers may say no when a boss asks to put tracking apps on their personal phone or computer. Settings where paid personal care services are provided are exempt. Each violation carries a fine of $100 to $500. The Maine House passed it 73-63 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 517, a bill about fake audio and video in campaign ads. A political ad that uses fake audio, video, or images of a candidate must carry a warning saying the content was changed. The law calls this synthetic media, meaning a doctored clip that would fool a reasonable person about what a candidate said or did. Ads that are clearly jokes or parody do not need the warning. Neither do small edits like cropping or color fixes. Breaking this rule can cost up to five times what was spent on the ad, and the usual chance to fix the problem within 10 days and avoid a penalty does not apply. A broadcaster or newspaper is only liable if it ran the ad knowing it contained synthetic media. The Maine House passed it 73-65 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 1937, a bill about free and reduced hospital care. Maine hospitals must run a program that helps patients pay, and must give free care to patients whose family income is at or below twice the federal poverty level. The federal poverty level is the income line the government uses to decide who counts as poor. A hospital has 45 days to answer a completed application. Patients earning up to four times that line must be offered a payment plan that never takes more than 4 percent of their monthly family income. The Maine Senate passed it 21-14 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the Senate's version of LD 598, giving up a House amendment the Senate had refused. The law makes an employer with at least 10 regular workers pay a worker who reports for a shift the employer then cancels or cuts short. The pay is two hours at the worker's regular rate, or the scheduled shift's pay if that is less. An employer who made a documented good-faith try to reach the worker owes nothing. Bad weather, disasters, worker illness, and workplace injury are also excepted. Seasonal workers and union public employees are not covered. The House agreed 76-69, and the bill became law without the governor's signature as Public Law Chapter 418.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against accepting the Senate's version of LD 598 and against dropping the House's own amendment. The bill makes an employer with at least 10 regular workers pay a worker who shows up for a shift the employer then cancels or cuts short. The pay is two hours at the regular rate, or the scheduled shift's pay if that is less. Bad weather, disasters, worker illness, and workplace injury are excepted, as is a documented good-faith try to reach the worker. The House agreed 76-69, and the bill became law without the governor's signature as Public Law Chapter 418.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 598, a bill about pay when a shift is cancelled. If a worker shows up for a scheduled shift and the boss then cancels it or cuts it short, the boss must still pay them. The pay is two hours at the worker's normal rate, or the pay for the shift they were scheduled for, whichever is less. This covers employers with at least 10 workers. It does not apply when bad weather, a disaster, the worker's own illness, or a workplace injury stops the work. Seasonal-industry workers and public employees covered by a union contract are also outside the law. A boss who made a documented, good-faith try to call the worker off does not owe the pay. But if the worker still turns up, the boss must give them duties they can do, and must pay them if there is no work to assign. This was the final passage vote. The Maine Senate passed it 18-16 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 2231, a bill about mobile home parks and manufactured housing. The owner of a mobile home park may raise lot rent only once a year. Lot rent is what a homeowner pays for the ground their home sits on. Residents can force the owner into mediation, a meeting with a neutral third person, when a rent increase runs more than 1 point above the region's rise in everyday prices. If the park owner demands a secrecy agreement during that mediation, the owner is treated as acting in bad faith. The law also cuts the minimum lot sizes towns may require for new or expanded mobile home parks, and lets a manufactured home or tiny home be converted into real estate and sold by deed. The Maine House passed it 78-67 and it became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the committee's ought-to-pass report on LD 1016, the step that moved the bill toward passage. The bill charges the buyer of a manufactured housing community or mobile home park $10,000 for each lot. The buyer pays when the deed is recorded, and the money goes to a new state fund. That fund helps homeowners, resident co-ops, and nonprofits buy these parks and keep them affordable. State and city housing authorities are exempt, as are co-ops of the home owners and buyers worth under $50 million. The version voted on here started the fee on January 1, 2026. The House then amended it to drop that start date and to require a sworn net-worth statement. The report was accepted 75-65 and the bill became law as Public Law Chapter 398.
judgments.nay_description: Voted against accepting the committee's ought-to-pass report on LD 1016. The bill charges the buyer of a manufactured housing community or mobile home park $10,000 for each lot, paid when the deed is recorded. The money goes to a state fund that helps homeowners, resident co-ops, and nonprofits buy these parks and keep them affordable. Housing authorities, co-ops of the home owners, and buyers worth under $50 million do not pay. The version voted on here would have started the fee on January 1, 2026, a date the House later removed. The report was accepted 75-65 and the bill became law as Public Law Chapter 398.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to accept the House's final version of LD 1016, the last contested vote on the bill. Buyers worth under $50 million are exempt too, counting related companies, and must file a sworn statement of net worth. The Senate agreed 18-15, and the governor signed it as Public Law Chapter 398.

judgments.yea_description: Voted yes on LD 2176, a bill about tenants' private information. A landlord may not hand out a tenant's or applicant's private information without their permission when the point is to scare or pressure them into moving out, and there is no real business reason for it. Doing so costs the landlord $1,000. The bill also raises the fine for a landlord who walks into a tenant's home without proper notice from $100 to $250. The Maine Senate passed it 20-14 and it became law.
